blocks.text: Florence Bourgeois is the director of Paris Photo and Anna Planas is its artistic director. Interview.
The Bicentennial of photography is an opportunity to look back over two centuries of history, but also to question the medium today. How is Paris Photo approaching this year’s edition?

Florence Bourgeois: Paris Photo will be the first international event to celebrate the Bicentennial of photography, under the patronage of the Ministry of Culture. We are delighted to take part in this celebration of photographic creation and heritage, which will unfold in France and abroad starting September 2026. For the occasion, we will host the Centre Pompidou at the fair, which will present a selection of around one hundred works by thirty artists from its collection, including recent acquisitions made specifically for this Bicentennial exhibition.

Anna Planas: This anniversary is not only an occasion to look back at the history of photography, but also to consider its transformations. For us, it is also a way to welcome collectors who specialize in other fields and to invite a broad public to discover and celebrate photography. Throughout the Grand Palais, visitors will be able to walk through two hundred years of photography by following a Bicentennial trail, from nineteenth-century works to those of today. From the entrance of the Grand Palais, Thomas Ruff will set the tone with a retrospective installation conceived as an “open book,” which reflects his experimental approach to the image. Throughout the fair, several galleries will show examples of the earliest photographic processes, such as calotypes, daguerreotypes and photograms, while others will offer a rereading of history through contemporary works.
What shapes an edition of Paris Photo?

Florence: For almost thirty years, Paris Photo has evolved with the market, thanks to the close relationships we maintain with participating galleries, international institutions, collectors and a very loyal public. Every year, we work with the galleries to renew the content of the fair and to bring forward new artists, new practices and new points of view.

Our travels and the encounters we have throughout the year are essential to understanding how artistic practices and the market are evolving. They directly inform how we approach each edition. This dialogue continues with our selection committee: beyond choosing the participating galleries, our discussions feed our thinking about the evolution of the fair.

Anna: We also invite curators to conceive specific sectors. What interests us is what happens when someone brings a different perspective from our own. The Voices and Digital sectors are built from this exchange: the curators introduce artists and ways of looking that broaden our approach to photography across the fair.

The Conversations program rests on this same logic of collaboration. It brings together figures from museums, research and the art market, and puts artists, gallerists and publishers in dialogue with people from other disciplines, notably film and fashion. The Éditions sector extends these exchanges further through the signings, the Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards and the book talks organized by Printed Matter.
What makes photography of interest to collectors today?

Florence: Photography is now an integral part of contemporary art collections around the world. And collecting photography can today cover very different realities: a vintage print, a complete series, archives, or a work at the crossroads of photography and other media. Beyond this diversity, photography holds a special place in our relationship to the world: it never stops renewing the way we see and understand it.

Anna: Photography has undergone profound transformations since the creation of Paris Photo, in visual, technical, aesthetic and conceptual terms. They have created a fertile and stimulating artistic ground for the medium, which keeps evolving, widening its place in the market and, in a way, strengthening its recognition.
Paris Photo November 12–15, 2026 | Grand Palais 1 p.m. – 8 p.m. (Sunday 7 p.m.) 3 avenue du Général Eisenhower 75008 Paris, France www.parisphoto.com
